title: Nigel Farage referred to watchdog over 'gifts' from crypto investor 'Posh George'

full_text: Nigel Farage referred to UK standards watchdog over undeclared gifts from crypto investor George Cottrell Mon 6 Jul 2026 at 12:35pm In short: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has been referred to the UK parliament's standards watchdog after reportedly failing to declare assistance from a crypto investor known as "Posh George" in the lead-up to the 2024 election. Mr Farage is already under investigation by the watchdog over a similarly undeclared donation made by a different crypto investor of 5 million pounds ($9.6 million), which Mr Farage says was an unconditional gift. What's next? Mr Farage, whose Reform UK party is topping national opinion polls, is awaiting the outcome of the first investigation, which could see him suspended from the House of Commons if a serious breach is found. Nigel Farage, the leader of Britain's anti-immigration Reform UK party, has been referred to the UK parliament's standards watchdog following reports he failed to declare assistance from a wealthy backer previously imprisoned in the US for wire fraud. The Sunday Times reported yesterday that, in the lead-up to the 2024 general election, Mr Farage was provided with security services, social media support and accommodation by George Cottrell, a 32-year-old cryptocurrency investor who served eight months in prison after being caught agreeing to launder money for drug traffickers in an FBI sting operation. Known by the nickname "Posh George", Mr Cottrell later served as chief of staff to Mr Farage during his time as the leader of UKIP, and has often been seen by the far-right politician's side over the past decade, including during the 2024 campaign. Mr Farage released a statement on Sunday evening calling himself the victim of an "establishment hit job", insisting no rules had been broken. "I have done no wrongdoing, followed the rules and I am now considering legal action against the Sunday Times," Mr Farage said. "It's now clear the establishment will stop at nothing to hurt Reform — we want to smash their cosy consensus." But Liberal Democrat MP Josh Babarinde, who wrote to the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards on Sunday calling for an investigation into the allegations, said Mr Farage was "not being straight with the British people about who controls him". "Given the value and nature of the support described, there is a serious question as to whether Mr Farage met his obligations under the Code of Conduct for MPs," he said in a letter he made public on X. "This is not an isolated concern." Mr Farage is already under investigation by the standards watchdog over separate allegations he should have declared a 5 million pound ($9.6 million) donation from a different cryptocurrency investor, billionaire Christopher Harborne, before the 2024 poll. The Reform UK leader has said the 5 million pounds he received from the Thailand-based investor was an unconditional gift that was given to him before he announced he would stand as an MP in 2024, and was thus exempt from disclosure rules. Mr Farage is awaiting the outcome of the investigation, which could lead to his suspension from the House of Commons if a serious breach is found to have taken place. A suspension of 10 days or more could also trigger a recall petition, potentially forcing a by-election in his constituency of Clacton. Reform UK has topped national opinion polls for more than a year, making Mr Farage a possible future prime minister after the next general election, which is scheduled for no later than August 2029. Britain tightens rules on overseas donations The renewed focus on Mr Farage's finances came as Britain's Labour government announced it would tighten the rules that govern overseas political donations, part of its efforts to stop foreign money influencing domestic elections. The government last year ordered a review into foreign financial interference in politics, after a former Reform UK politician was jailed for taking bribes to make pro-Russia speeches and statements. The review found Britain faced a persistent problem of foreign countries, including Russia, China and Iran, trying to influence and undermine the country's democracy. From now on, candidates in British elections will be required to declare any donations of more than 2,230 pounds ($4,292) received before becoming a candidate, and to prove any pre-candidacy funding had come from legitimate sources, Housing Minister Steve Reed said on Monday. "By holding overseas donors to tougher standards and requiring candidates to prove where their funding comes from, we are taking world-leading action to protect the integrity of our elections and tackle the threats we face from abroad," Mr Reed said. The tougher rules also mean individuals moving to the UK from overseas now have to live permanently in the UK for a year before they can make a political donation of 100,000 pounds ($192,480) or more, while donations from companies are to be assessed against past post-tax profits rather than revenue, helping to ensure donations are made only by legitimate businesses with links to the UK. Those rules build on earlier reforms announced in March, which capped donations by Britons living overseas at 100,000 pounds per year, and introduced a ban on crypto donations until a system to regulate them effectively is established. ABC/Reuters
